name: Binary and denary
rule: Each bit in an 8-bit binary number has a place value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. To turn binary into denary, add the place values that have a 1 under them. To turn denary into binary, take the biggest place value that fits, subtract it, and repeat with what is left.
trick: Write 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above the bits before you do anything else. Most mistakes come from counting places in your head.

another.text: Binary is like paying with coins worth 128p, 64p, 32p and so on, where you can use each coin once or not at all. A 1 means you used that coin.

walkthrough.board: Convert 01010110 to denary, then convert 86 back to binary.

steps.say: Write the place values over the bits: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

steps.ask: Which place values have a 1 under them?
Now go back the other way. What is the biggest place value that fits into 86?
What is the biggest place value that fits into 22?

steps.say: So the 1s go under 64, 16, 4 and 2, giving 01010110. Both directions agree.

questions.stem: What is 40 as an 8-bit binary number?

name: Hexadecimal
sub: One hex digit is four bits
rule: Hexadecimal (base 16) uses the digits 0 to 9 and then A to F for 10 to 15. One hex digit stands for exactly four bits (a nibble). To change binary to hex, split it into nibbles and convert each one using 8, 4, 2, 1. To change two-digit hex to denary, multiply the first digit by 16 and add the second.
trick: Learn A = 10 and F = 15; the letters in between count up from there.

another.text: Hex is a shorthand, like writing a dozen instead of twelve things one by one. Four bits squash into one symbol, so a long binary number gets much shorter.

walkthrough.board: Convert 1100 1001 to hexadecimal, then to denary.

steps.say: Split the byte into two nibbles: 1100 and 1001. Each nibble becomes one hex digit.

steps.ask: Using 8, 4, 2, 1, what is 1100?
steps.hint: 8 + 4 + 0 + 0. Then A is 10, B is 11, C is 12.

steps.ask: What is 1001?
So what is the hex number?
steps.then: Keep the nibbles in the same order as the binary.

steps.ask: Now to denary: C9 = 12 × 16 + 9 = ?

questions.stem: What is the hex number 2F in denary?

questions.why: 1110 is 14, which is E, and 0011 is 3.

name: Binary addition and shifts
rule: Add binary right to left, like column addition. 0 + 1 = 1. 1 + 1 = 10: write 0 and carry 1. 1 + 1 + 1 = 11: write 1 and carry 1. If a carry goes past the last bit, the answer does not fit: that is overflow. Shifting left by one place doubles a number; shifting right by one place halves it, and bits that fall off the end are lost.
trick: Check every answer in denary: convert both numbers, add them, and convert your binary answer back.

another.text: In binary you are only allowed 0 and 1, so the moment a column reaches 2 it is full, like a cup that overflows into the next cup along.
another.example:
1 + 1 = 2
Too much for one column
Write 0, carry 1

steps.ask: Start with the right-hand column: 1 + 1 = ?
steps.hint: 2 is not a binary digit. 2 in binary is 10.

steps.ask: Next column: 1 + 1 + the carried 1 = ?
steps.hint: Three 1s make 3, which is 11 in binary.

steps.ask: Next column: 0 + 1 + the carried 1 = ?
Last column: 0 + 0 + the carried 1 = ?
Read the answer from left to right. 0011 + 0111 = ?
Shifting 1010 one place left gives 10100. What did that do to 10?

questions.why: 3 + 5 = 8, which is 1000. The carries ripple all the way to the left.

questions.stem: What is 00011000 shifted right by 2 places?
questions.why: Two places right divides by 4: 24 becomes 6. 01100000 is a left shift.

name: File sizes and units
rule: 8 bits make 1 byte. 1,000 bytes make a kilobyte, 1,000 KB a megabyte and 1,000 MB a gigabyte (you may also see 1,024, written KiB, MiB and GiB). Image size in bits = width × height × colour depth. Sound size in bits = sample rate × bit depth × seconds. Divide bits by 8 to get bytes.
trick: Work it out in bits first, then divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for each step up.

examples.text: n bits per pixel give 2ⁿ colours

another.text: Bits are like single sweets, bytes are bags of 8 sweets, and kilobytes are boxes of 1,000 bags. To count boxes, first count the sweets, then bag them, then box them.

walkthrough.board: A 200 × 100 pixel image has a colour depth of 4 bits. What is its size in kilobytes?

steps.ask: How many pixels are there?
steps.hint: Multiply the width by the height.

steps.ask: Each pixel needs 4 bits. How many bits for the whole image?
To turn bits into bytes, divide by what?
With 1 KB = 1,000 bytes, how many kilobytes?

questions.stem: How many bits are there in 3 bytes?
A 10 × 10 pixel image uses 8 bits per pixel. What is its size in bytes?
questions.why: 100 pixels × 8 bits = 800 bits, and 800 ÷ 8 = 100 bytes. 800 is the size in bits.

name: Trace tables
sub: Run the code one line at a time
rule: A trace table has a column for each variable (and one for output) and a new row each time a value changes. Follow the code one line at a time, write down every new value as it is assigned, and check the loop condition every time round.
trick: Never run two lines in your head at once. Write each change down, even the boring ones, and the answer falls out of the last row.

examples.note: x becomes 7: write 7 in the x column
The loop body runs with i = 1, 2 and 3: three times

another.text: A trace table is like keeping score in a game: every time someone scores, you write the new total down instead of trying to remember it.

walkthrough.board: total ← 10. FOR i ← 1 TO 3: total ← total − i. ENDFOR. OUTPUT total

steps.ask: Before the loop starts, what is total?
First time round, i = 1. What does total become?
Second time round, i = 2. What does total become?
steps.hint: Take i away from the total you already have: 9 − 2.

steps.ask: Third time round, i = 3. What does total become?
Does the loop run again with i = 4?
What is output?

questions.stem: x ← 2, then x ← x × 3, then x ← x − 1. What is x now?
count ← 0. WHILE count < 3: count ← count + 1. ENDWHILE. How many times does the loop body run?
questions.why: count goes 1, 2, 3. When count is 3, count < 3 is false, so the loop stops after 3 runs.

name: AND, OR and NOT
rule: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT flips its single input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. A truth table lists every combination of inputs: 2 inputs need 4 rows, and each extra input doubles that. Work out brackets first.
trick: AND is strict (both), OR is easy-going (either). Anything AND 0 is 0; anything OR 1 is 1.

another.text: AND is like needing both a ticket and a wristband to get in. OR is like being let in with either one. NOT is saying the opposite.
another.example:
Ticket AND wristband: both needed
Ticket OR wristband: one is enough
NOT raining = dry

walkthrough.board: Q = (A OR B) AND (NOT C), with A = 0, B = 1, C = 0

steps.ask: First bracket: A OR B = 0 OR 1 = ?
steps.hint: OR needs only one input to be 1.

steps.ask: Second bracket: NOT C = NOT 0 = ?
Now combine them: 1 AND 1 = ?
If C were 1 instead, what would Q be?
steps.then: NOT C would be 0, and anything AND 0 is 0.

questions.why: AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1.

questions.stem: How many rows does a truth table for 5 inputs need?
